subject: a banana
facts: Bananas curve because they grow upwards, turning towards the sunlight as they get bigger.
A banana plant is not a tree; its trunk is made of tightly rolled leaves.
Most bananas sold in shops are one variety, grown as copies of the same plant.

subject: a potato
facts: In 1995, potatoes became the first vegetable ever grown in space, aboard a NASA shuttle.
A green patch on a potato means light reached it, which also builds up a natural poison.
Keeping potatoes in the fridge turns some of their starch into sugar, so they taste sweet.

subject: tea
facts: Black, green, white and oolong tea all come from the very same plant.
Weight for weight, dry tea leaves contain more caffeine than coffee beans.
The thin skin on top of a cup of tea comes from minerals in hard water.

subject: an egg
facts: An eggshell has thousands of tiny holes, so a growing chick can breathe through it.
Older eggs are easier to peel after boiling than very fresh ones.
The green ring around a boiled yolk appears when an egg has been cooked too long.

subject: an apple
facts: An apple floats in water because about a quarter of it is air.
Plant a seed from your favourite apple and the tree will grow a completely different apple.
One rotten apple really can spoil the rest, because it gives off a gas that speeds up ripening.

subject: a pencil
facts: The lead in a pencil has never been lead; it is graphite mixed with clay.
A thick pencil line can carry a tiny electric current, because graphite conducts electricity.
More clay makes a pencil harder and its line lighter, which is what the letters on it mean.

subject: a mirror
facts: A mirror doesn't really swap left and right; it swaps front and back.
Most mirrors are a very thin layer of metal, such as aluminium or silver, behind glass.
Mirrors are very slightly green, which you can see when two face each other.

subject: a smartphone
facts: Your phone knows which way up it is because a tiny sensor inside feels gravity.
Your phone's compass works using a tiny sensor that detects the Earth's magnetic field.
A second tiny microphone on your phone listens to background noise so it can remove it from calls.

subject: a fridge
facts: A fridge doesn't make cold; it moves heat from inside to the outside.
Leaving the fridge door open actually warms your kitchen up overall.
The small hole at the back of the inside is a drain for melted frost.

subject: a washing machine
facts: Many washing machines hide a heavy concrete block that stops them walking across the floor.
Most of the energy a hot wash uses goes on heating the water.
Using too much detergent can leave clothes dirtier, because leftover soap attracts dirt.

subject: toothpaste
facts: Orange juice tastes bitter after brushing because a foaming ingredient in toothpaste dulls your taste for sweetness.
Toothpaste scrubs your teeth with a very fine powder, often chalk or silica.
The foam doesn't do the cleaning; it just helps spread the toothpaste around your mouth.

subject: chocolate
facts: Chocolate melts in your mouth because cocoa butter melts just below body temperature.
The white film on old chocolate is only fat or sugar that rose to the surface.
Cocoa pods grow straight out of the trunk of the tree, not just on its branches.

subject: a coffee bean
facts: A coffee bean is the seed of a small red fruit called a coffee cherry.
Raw coffee beans are green and smell more like grass than coffee.
Dark roast coffee does not have more caffeine than light roast, even though it tastes stronger.

subject: salt
facts: Most of the salt mined in the world never reaches a plate; industry and icy roads use it.
A pinch of salt makes bitter food taste less bitter, even coffee.
Fancy sea salt and ordinary table salt contain about the same amount of sodium by weight.

subject: a dog
facts: Dogs have a third eyelid that sweeps across the eye to protect it.
Puppies are born both blind and deaf, and depend on smell and touch at first.
Sleeping dogs show the same kind of brain activity that people have when dreaming.

subject: a cactus
facts: The spines on a cactus are actually its leaves, changed over time to save water.
A cactus makes its food in its green stem, doing the job that leaves do on other plants.
A cactus breathes at night, keeping its tiny pores shut during the day to save water.

subject: a pair of jeans
facts: Jeans fade because the blue dye only coats the outside of each thread.
Jeans are paler on the inside because only one set of threads is dyed blue.
Look closely at denim and you'll see the threads run in tiny diagonal lines.

subject: a candle
facts: A candle doesn't burn solid wax; the flame burns the wax after it has turned to vapour.
In space, a candle flame becomes a round blue ball instead of a pointed shape.
You can relight a candle from a small distance by touching a flame to its smoke.

subject: a bicycle
facts: Riding a bike uses less energy per kilometre than walking the same distance.
A well-oiled bike chain passes on about 98 percent of your pedalling power.
Push a riderless bike hard enough and it can balance by itself for a while.

subject: milk
facts: Milk is white because tiny droplets of fat and other particles scatter all the light.
Skimmed milk can look slightly blue because most of its fat has been removed.
Most milk is forced through tiny holes at high pressure so the cream doesn't rise to the top.

subject: a mango
facts: Mangoes are related to cashews and poison ivy, and their peel can give some people a rash.
A mango can be perfectly ripe while still green, so colour is a poor guide.
India grows more mangoes than any other country, around 40 percent of the world's crop.

subject: a glass bottle
facts: Glass is made mostly of ordinary sand, melted at very high temperatures.
A glass bottle can be recycled again and again without losing its quality.
Beer bottles are often brown because the colour blocks light that would spoil the taste.

subject: a door lock
facts: The bumps on a key lift tiny pins inside the lock to exactly the right height.
Many house keys are made of brass, a metal that naturally kills germs on its surface.
Locksmiths often use graphite powder rather than oil, because oil collects dirt inside a lock.

subject: a zip
facts: The slider has a Y-shaped channel inside that presses the two rows of teeth together.
A stuck zip often frees up if you rub a pencil along its teeth.
One of the earliest zips was invented to fasten boots, not clothes.

subject: a banknote
facts: Many banknotes are not paper at all, but cotton or thin plastic.
Many banknotes have raised ink you can feel, so people can check them by touch.
Hold many banknotes up to the light and a hidden thread and picture appear inside.

subject: a battery
facts: A dead AA battery bounces higher than a fresh one when dropped on its end.
Batteries slowly lose their charge even when they are never used.
Keeping ordinary batteries in the fridge doesn't help, and damp can even damage them.

subject: a toilet
facts: The bend in a toilet pipe holds water that stops smells coming back up.
A toilet flush works by siphon: rushing water pulls the bowl empty all at once.
Flushing with the lid up sends a fine spray of tiny droplets into the air.

subject: sticky tape
facts: Peeling sticky tape in a vacuum gives off X-rays, which scientists measured in 2008.
Sticky tape works through pressure alone; its glue never dries or hardens to hold.
Clear tape turns yellow with age because its glue slowly breaks down.

subject: a sheet of paper
facts: Fold an A4 sheet in half and it keeps exactly the same shape, just smaller.
Paper can only be recycled about five to seven times before its fibres get too short.
Old paper turns yellow because a natural substance from the wood breaks down in light and air.

subject: rice
facts: Rice left out at room temperature can make you ill even after it is reheated.
Rice is the main food of more than half the people in the world.
Cooling cooked rice changes its starch, so your body digests it more slowly.
